thread.title: Apple, Nike, Starbucks Could Be Victims in Trade War

author: Reshma Kapadia
title: Apple, Nike, Starbucks Could Be Victims in Trade War
text:
President Donald Trump is expected to announce tariffs on up to $50 billion of Chinese imports against China later today, a move that analysts expect will not go unanswered by China. Untangling the global value chain to gauge just who would be hit—and by how much—is complex, but some see the move as bad news for several large U.S. agricultural and consumer companies.
The move will only amplify concerns of a trade war. Agriculture could be one target , with China, the biggest buyer of U.S. soybeans, potentially bypassing the U.S. and favoring other exporters like Brazil and Argentina, writes David Riedel, who runs the emerging-markets-focused Riedel Research . A threat to U.S. agricultural exports could also hurt companies like Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) and farm-equipment maker Deere (DE), Riedel writes in a note.
China could also retaliate by making its much sought-after consumers harder to reach by U.S. companies, which have staked much of their growth on emerging market consumers. “Beijing has a long history of initiating or supporting consumer boycotts in support of national objectives,” Riedel writes. In 2012, China supported a consumer boycott of Japanese brands after tensions flared over the Daioyu/Senkaku islands, Riedel said.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping Illustration: Bloomberg News Japanese-made cars in China saw a sharp drop in sales though it lasted just a couple quarters, Riedel said. This time around, consumer brands that have made headway into China, like Nike (NKE), Apple (AAPL), Yum! Brands (YUM), and Starbucks (SBUX) could take a hit.
In a separate note by Yardeni Research’s Ed Yardeni this morning, the strategist said it is tough to gauge the impact of tariffs because it’s not crystal clear where S&P 500 companies’ goods are sold geographically. Only about half disclose whether they have foreign sales—and of those, 43% of their sales were generated abroad in 2016, Yardeni writes.
Those companies that do offer more granular data indicate that Asia represented about 8.5% of foreign sales, with Europe close behind at 8.1%. Energy, technology, and materials are the three sectors that get more than half of their total sales from abroad.
UBS economist Li Zeng makes a similar point on the difficulty in untangling the global value chain to get a good sense of who would be impacted, but notes that over 40% of the U.S. imports from China are tech products and electrical equipment—making them a potentially natural target.
Zeng notes that the U.S. imported $107 billion in technology products from China in 2014, though based on the World Input-Output Database, he estimates that only $80 billion was really from China, with another $27 billion sourced from its global value chain partners—those in Korea, Taiwan, and Japan. That underscores the complexity and potential ripples from a trade move in today’s interconnected world.
